title: Classification Keys
seo_title: Year 6 Science: Classification Keys Worksheets (Branching Keys for Animals)
standard_code: Year 6: Living things and their habitats
standard_text: Describe how living things are classified into broad groups according to common observable characteristics and based on similarities and differences, including micro-organisms, plants and animals. Give reasons for classifying plants and animals based on specific characteristics.
meta_desc: Free Year 6 science worksheets on classification keys: follow a branching key, find the question that separates two animals and write good key questions. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Yes or no, branch by branch.
key_sub: Each question splits the group until one living thing is left.
body_html:
How to think about it

A key asks yes/no questions that split a group again and again until one living thing is left.

  • Start at question 1. Follow Yes or No to the next question.
  • Good questions are about features you can see or count: legs, wings, a shell, fur, feathers.
  • Bad questions are opinions (Is it pretty?) or vague (Is it big?).
Example

Snail, slug, spider, bee. First question: Does it have legs?

Yes: spider, bee. No: snail, slug

Answer: It splits the group into two.

Example

Snail or slug? Which question?

Only one has a shell

Answer: Does it have a shell?

Common mistakes

  • Following the Yes branch when the answer is No.
  • Using opinion questions.
  • Asking a question that does not split the group.

faq.q: How do you use a classification key?
faq.a: Start at the first question, answer yes or no, and follow that branch to the next question until you reach the name of one living thing.

faq.q: What makes a good key question?
faq.a: It has a clear yes or no answer about a feature you can see or count, such as legs, wings or a shell, and it splits the group into two.

faq.q: Why do keys use yes/no questions?
faq.a: Two choices make each step simple and mean that anyone using the key gets the same answer.
